metadata.note: Passenger rail at Eau Claire, Wisconsin -- a city that had a great deal of it and now has none. The line reached Eau Claire in 1870 and became part of the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis and Omaha Railway, the 'Omaha Road', when that company was formed by merger in 1880; by 1884 three railroads were running fourteen passenger trains a day through the city, the Omaha Road alone accounting for six between Chicago and St. Paul. Its best-known train was the Chicago and North Western's 400, which began on Jan 2 1935 and took its name from covering roughly 400 miles between Chicago and St. Paul in 400 minutes, stops included. Renamed the Twin Cities 400 in 1941 and streamlined throughout, it made its last call at Eau Claire on July 23 1963, and that was the end of passenger service on the line. The 1893 depot at 324 Putnam Street -- Charles Sumner Frost's Richardsonian Romanesque design in Lake Superior brownstone -- was demolished in 1987 despite being on the National Register of Historic Places. This layer draws the Omaha Road corridor the trains actually used, Wyeville west through Eau Claire to the Twin Cities; the 400's run east of Wyeville over the Chicago and North Western to Milwaukee and Chicago is not drawn here.
sources: https://www.streamlinerschedules.com/concourse/track4/cnw400194106.html (Chicago and North Western '400', June 1941 timetable). Mileposts from Chicago used as the route check: Chicago 0.0, Evanston 12.0, Racine 61.9, Milwaukee 85.0, South Beaver Dam 148.0, Adams 209.5, Wyeville 238.9, Eau Claire 323.1, St. Paul 408.6, Minneapolis 419.2.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Cities_400 (first service Jan 2 1935; ran on the Chicago and North Western from Chicago through Evanston, Racine, Milwaukee, Adams to Wyeville, and on the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis and Omaha from Wyeville through Merrillan and Eau Claire to St. Paul Union Depot and the Great Northern Depot at Minneapolis; re-equipped 1939 with EMD E3A locomotives and lightweight streamlined cars; E6 power and the Twin Cities 400 name from 1941, E7 from 1947, E8 in the 1950s; derailed between Knapp and Menomonie July 30 1959, injuring 50 of 115 passengers, with trees along the elevated railway preventing the coaches from plummeting; last service July 23 1963).

https://volumeone.org/news/2016/02/19/253300-passenger-rail-photos-from-eau-claire-in-the-mid and https://minds.wisconsin.edu/handle/1793/39007 ('Last Stop Eau Claire: The Discontinuation of the Twin Cities 400'): the Omaha Road line reached Eau Claire in 1870; as early as 1884 Eau Claire was served by three separate railroads operating 14 passenger trains per day, the Omaha Road alone running six daily through Eau Claire between Chicago and St. Paul; the Twin Cities 400 made its last stop in Eau Claire July 23 1963 and passenger service on the line ceased that year.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eau_Claire_station_(Wisconsin) (the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis & Omaha depot, a subsidiary of the Chicago and North Western, built 1893 at 324 Putnam Street to a Charles Sumner Frost design in Richardsonian Romanesque style using Lake Superior brownstone; passenger service on the line ceased 1963; the depot was demolished in 1987 despite remaining on the National Register of Historic Places).
metadata.not_yet_sourced: All frequencies are estimates. The two railroads other than the Omaha Road that made up Eau Claire's fourteen daily trains in 1884 were not identified, so only the Omaha Road corridor is drawn. The company that actually built the line into Eau Claire in 1870, before the 1880 merger created the Omaha Road, was not established either, so the 1870-1880 segment is attributed to 'predecessors of the Omaha Road'. Nor are the Omaha Road's other named trains through Eau Claire covered here, only the 400. Modern proposals to restore Twin Cities-Eau Claire service are out of scope for this layer.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API, shortest-path search over the OSM rail graph between the towns on the route, run three ways (plain rail, abandoned-preferring, and abandoned-preferring with a wide gap stitch) and merged. West of Eau Claire much of the old Omaha Road roadbed is now the Chippewa River and Red Cedar state trails, so that half depends on OSM's abandoned-railway coverage -- the abandoned-preferring pass is what traced it.

Legs were validated by SPAN against the 1941 timetable mileposts. All three spans traced on real track with no straight-line approximations: Wyeville-Eau Claire 135.2 km against 135.5 booked (1.00x), Eau Claire-St. Paul 145.2 against 137.6 (1.06x), St. Paul-Minneapolis 15.4 against 17.1 (0.90x). Total 296 km against the booked 290 km Wyeville to Minneapolis, a 1.02x match.

Per-span tracing result: ok Wyeville -> Eau Claire: 135.2km vs 135.5km booked (1.00x) [rail] via Merrillan, Humbird, Fairchild, Augusta, Fall Creek | ok Eau Claire -> Saint Paul: 145.2km vs 137.6km booked (1.06x) [abandoned] via Elk Mound, Menomonie, Knapp, Baldwin, Hudson | ok Saint Paul -> Minneapolis: 15.4km vs 17.1km booked (0.90x) [rail]

The Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis and Omaha Railway was formed by merger in 1880 and took the line over (see chicago_stpaul_minneapolis_omaha.geojson for the Omaha Road's western end); frequency estimated, unsourced

By 1884 Eau Claire was served by three separate railroads running fourteen passenger trains a day between them, the Omaha Road alone working six daily through the city between Chicago and St. Paul. Its 1893 depot at 324 Putnam Street, by Charles Sumner Frost, was Richardsonian Romanesque in Lake Superior brownstone; frequency estimated, unsourced

properties.speed_source: estimated from the train's own billing -- 400 minutes for the 400-odd miles between Chicago and St. Paul, about 60 mph including stops; unsourced for other eras

segments.note: The 400 began Jan 2 1935, named for the 400 minutes it took to cover the roughly 400 miles between St. Paul and Chicago, station stops included. East of Wyeville it ran on the Chicago and North Western through Adams, Milwaukee and Racine to Chicago; that portion is not drawn here; frequency estimated, unsourced

Re-equipped in 1939 with EMD E3A locomotives and lightweight streamlined cars, renamed the Twin Cities 400 in 1941 as the North Western spread the 400 name across a family of trains, with E6, E7 and later E8 power. On July 30 1959 it derailed between Knapp and Menomonie, injuring 50 of its 115 passengers; trees along the elevated roadbed kept the cars from going over the side. The last one called at Eau Claire on July 23 1963, ending passenger service on the line; frequency estimated, unsourced
